audience: undergraduate computer science; spoken explanation of 1-3 minutes

key_points.text: Virtual memory gives each process its own private, contiguous virtual address space that is independent of the size and layout of physical RAM.
key_points.partial_if: says programs 'think they have more memory' without the per-process address space

key_points.text: Virtual addresses are translated to physical addresses by the MMU (hardware) using page tables kept by the OS; a TLB caches recent translations.
key_points.partial_if: mentions translation or page tables but not who does it, or the TLB alone

key_points.text: Paging: memory is divided into fixed-size pages (virtual) and frames (physical); only the pages in use need to be in RAM, the rest can stay on disk (swap / backing store), loaded on demand.
key_points.partial_if: mentions pages or disk storage without explaining that only needed pages are in RAM

key_points.text: A page fault happens when a process touches a page not in RAM; the OS loads it from disk, evicting another page with a replacement policy (e.g. LRU) if RAM is full.
key_points.partial_if: mentions page faults by name only

key_points.text: Benefits: programs larger than RAM and more processes can run, processes are isolated and protected from each other, and memory such as shared libraries can be shared.
Cost: disk is far slower than RAM, so too many page faults cause thrashing, where the system spends most of its time paging.
key_points.partial_if: says it 'can be slow' without the reason

misconceptions.text: Virtual memory is just the swap or page file, i.e. using the hard disk as extra RAM.
Virtual memory makes the computer faster or makes RAM faster.
Virtual addresses are the same as physical addresses, or all processes share one address space.
